hints: Picture the starting point as separated gaseous ions, $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g})$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g})$, and the end point as one mole of solid lattice, then think which direction defines lattice energy.
walkthrough:
Fix the exact start and end states**
Think of lattice formation in the exothermic direction. You start with infinitely separated gaseous ions, for $\text{CaCl}_2$ that is $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g}) + 2\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g})$, and you finish with one mole of solid, $\text{CaCl}_2(\text{s})$. The energy released in that step is the lattice energy, so always quote one mole of solid from gaseous ions.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of solid ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions.

hints: Sketch a Born-Haber cycle with $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ as the direct route and atomisation, ionisation energies, electron affinities and lattice energy as the indirect route.
Remember to multiply the chlorine atomisation and electron affinity values by two because the formula is $\text{CaCl}_2$.
walkthrough:
Link formation to the Born-Haber route**
By Hess law, forming $\text{CaCl}_2(\text{s})$ directly from elements equals forming it via atoms then gaseous ions then solid. So $$\Delta H_f^\ominus = \Delta H_{at}^\ominus(\text{Ca}) + IE_1 + IE_2 + 2\Delta H_{at}^\ominus(\text{Cl}) + 2EA_1 + \Delta H_{latt}^\ominus$$

Substitute carefully with the factor of two**
Put the Table 1.1 numbers in: $$\Delta H_f^\ominus = (+193) + (+590) + (+1150) + (2 \times +121) + (2 \times -364) + (-2237)$$ That gives $+193 + 590 + 1150 + 242 - 728 - 2237 = -790 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. The large negative lattice energy dominates, making formation strongly exothermic.

hints: Compare the size of a Br atom with a Cl atom and think how distance of the outer shell from the nucleus affects attraction for an incoming electron.
walkthrough:
Reason from size to attraction**
First electron affinity is energy released when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons: $\text{Br}(\text{g}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Br}^{-}(\text{g})$. Bromine is below chlorine, so its outer shell is further out with more shielding. The incoming electron feels weaker nuclear attraction, so less energy is released. That means a less negative value than $-364 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, which is $-342 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Final answer: Tick $-342 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Br atom is larger than Cl atom so incoming electron is further from nucleus, experiences less attraction and less energy is released.

hints: For solution, focus on the change from one mole of solid solute to aqueous ions in water.
For hydration, focus on the change from one mole of gaseous ions to aqueous ions surrounded by water molecules.
walkthrough:
Separate solid dissolving from gas hydrating**
Solution starts with the solid: $\text{CaCl}_2(\text{s})$ plus water gives $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{aq})$. So it is the enthalpy change when one mole of solid dissolves in water.

Picture water surrounding a gaseous ion**
Hydration starts with an already gaseous ion, for example $\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g})$, which becomes surrounded by water molecules to give $\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{aq})$. So it is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water. It is always exothermic because new ion-dipole bonds to water form.

Final answer: Enthalpy change of solution: enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves in water.
Enthalpy change of hydration: enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form aqueous ions.

hints: Write the Hess cycle linking $\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus$ to breaking the lattice (+ reverse of lattice energy) followed by hydrating $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and two $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions.
Rearrange to solve for $\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-})$ and remember to divide the remainder by two.
walkthrough:
Build the solution cycle**
Dissolving involves two stages. Break the lattice back to gaseous ions, which is the reverse of lattice formation: $-\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus = +2237 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Then hydrate all the gaseous ions. So $$\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus = -\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus + \Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-})$$

Insert numbers and isolate chloride**
$$-83 = (+2237) + (-1650) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-})$$ Rearranging: $$2\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-}) = -83 -2237 + 1650 = -670$$ Therefore $$\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-}) = -335 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The division by two is essential because there are two moles of chloride per mole of $\text{CaCl}_2$.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus = -\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus + \Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-})$
$2\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-}) = -83 -2237 + 1650$ wait sign corrected: $-83 = +2237 -1650 + 2\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-})$, so $\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus(\text{Cl}^{-}) = -335 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Write the equation $\text{Ca}(\text{s}) + \text{F}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CaF}_2(\text{s})$ and count moles of gas on each side to judge disorder.
walkthrough:
Count disorder from gas to ordered solid**
The synthesis is $\text{Ca}(\text{s}) + \text{F}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CaF}_2(\text{s})$. You lose one mole of highly disordered gas and make a highly ordered solid lattice. Fewer particles free to move means less disorder, so $\Delta S^\ominus$ is negative.
Final answer: Negative, because gas is converted to solid / number of gas molecules decreases so disorder decreases.

hints: Recall $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$ and think what happens to $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ when $\Delta S^\ominus$ is negative and $T$ rises.
Link a more positive $\Delta G^\ominus$ to decreasing feasibility for the forward synthesis.
walkthrough:
See how temperature weights the entropy term**
Use $$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$$ Here $\Delta H^\ominus = -1214 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (favourable) but $\Delta S^\ominus$ is negative. So $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ is positive and grows larger as $T$ increases.

Predict feasibility**
At low $T$, the very negative $\Delta H^\ominus$ dominates and $\Delta G^\ominus$ is negative, so synthesis is feasible. At higher $T$, the positive $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ term outweighs $\Delta H^\ominus$, $\Delta G^\ominus$ becomes positive and the synthesis becomes less feasible.

Final answer: As $T$ increases, $T\Delta S^\ominus$ becomes more negative so $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ becomes more positive. $\Delta G^\ominus$ becomes less negative / more positive so reaction becomes less feasible.
